title: Rebekah says "I will go" (Genesis 24:57–58)
hook: her family asks her, and she chooses for herself

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chesed, kindness past what's owed, and ten thirsty camels. Your line: water the camels too.

Rebekah runs home and tells her family about the stranger at the well. Her brother Laban sees the gold bracelets, and invites the servant in. Food is set out, and the servant says: I won't eat until I've told you why I'm here. And he tells the whole story again, every detail: the prayer, the camels, the water. The rabbis noticed how long the Torah lets him talk, and said even the everyday speech of the patriarchs' servants is precious. The family agrees to the match. But in the morning, when the servant wants to leave, her mother and brother hesitate: let her stay with us a while, ten days at least. Don't hold me back, the servant says. Then the family does something the rabbis would later build a law on.
screen: `THE WHOLE STORY, TOLD AGAIN.` → `STAY TEN DAYS.` → `DON'T HOLD ME BACK.`

segments.voice: In the old JPS translation, they say: "We will call the damsel, and inquire at her mouth." They ask her directly: "Wilt thou go with this man?" She answers in one Hebrew word, elech: "I will go." Two things to notice. First, the asking. Rashi, the medieval commentator, reads this verse as a law: from here we learn that a woman may not be married off without her consent. Jewish law, as it developed, holds that a grown woman's marriage needs her own yes. The Torah could have skipped her answer. Instead it pauses to show someone asking her first. Second, the answer. Some commentators notice that Rebekah's yes sounds like Abraham's call: she, too, leaves her land, her birthplace and her father's house, for a man and a place she's never seen. She goes before she knows, just as he did. Her family sends her off with a blessing: our sister, may you become thousands upon thousands. At the bedeken, a Jewish wedding custom, those words are said to the bride as her veil is lowered. At the chapter's end, she arrives. Isaac has gone out to the field at evening, the Torah says, to meditate. She sees him from her camel and veils herself. He brings her into his mother Sarah's tent, and he loves her, the Torah says plainly, and he is comforted after his mother's death. And it started with a question: will you go?
screen: `INQUIRE AT HER MOUTH.` · `ELECH — I WILL GO.` · `NO MARRIAGE WITHOUT HER YES.` · `SHE LEAVES, LIKE ABRAHAM.` · then, large: `WILT THOU GO WITH THIS MAN?`

segments.voice: Think of a good invitation you keep not answering: a dinner you've been putting off, a class, a trip, a phone call, a new friendship, a volunteer shift. Notice what holds you back, tiredness, fear, habit, then picture answering like Rebekah, with one short word: I'll go. If you pray, you can ask for a clear yes.
Elech, Hebrew for I will go, Rebekah's whole answer. Her family asks her, and she chooses her own road in a single word.
Your line: ask her first. One word, elech, and she was on her way. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Jewish weddings that keep the bedeken, the veiling of the bride, the blessing Rebekah's family gave her is said over the bride; Jewish law requires the bride's own consent to the marriage.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 24:57 and 24:58.
Rashi on 24:57: 'from here we learn that a woman is not married off except with her consent' (also Kiddushin 2b/41a). Confirm.
Blessing of 24:60 said at the bedeken: common Ashkenazi practice; not universal. The script says 'at many Jewish weddings'. Confirm.
Genesis Rabbah 60:8 on the servant's speech. Confirm.
'First time the Torah says a husband loved his wife' (24:67): confirm.
Parallel between Rebekah's leaving and Abraham's lech lecha: noted by several commentators; confirm.
Title and word contain quotation marks as given by the index.

Reviewer softened 'Jewish law holds to that: a marriage needs the woman's own yes' to 'as it developed, holds that a grown woman's marriage needs her own yes'. Classical halakha let a father betroth a minor daughter (Kiddushin 41a discourages it), and some commentators read 24:57 as asking only whether she would leave now, not consent to the match. Confirm framing.
Lasuach in 24:63 ('to meditate', JPS 1917) is read by the rabbis as prayer (Berakhot 26b); others read 'to walk'. Script keeps 'to meditate'. Confirm.
